draft.title: Generalisations and predictions
card: Generalisation
A statement that holds for most cases in the data. It describes a pattern, but a few places may not fit it.
Prediction
A statement that extends a trend into the future. It says what is likely to happen, not what has happened.
A prediction is less certain the further ahead it goes. Conditions can change, and small errors grow over a longer time.
A good generalisation uses words such as most or many, and does not claim every case. A good prediction says how far ahead it looks.
draft.remember: A generalisation sums up most of the data. A prediction extends the trend, and it gets less certain the further ahead it looks.

a.q: A student reviews data for 20 towns. Fourteen towns lost population over ten years. Which statement is a generalisation?
opts: Most of these towns lost population over ten years
These towns will lose more people by next year
Every one of these towns lost population over ten years
These towns will have almost no people in 100 years
a.why: Fourteen of 20 is most of the cases, so the statement holds for most of the data. The statement about every town is wrong because six towns did not lose population. The other two look ahead, so they are predictions.
a.clue: Which one describes the data already collected and does not claim every case?

b.q: Rainfall in a Tasmanian catchment has fallen each year for eight years. Which prediction is most likely to be reliable?
opts: Rainfall will keep falling slightly next year
Rainfall will keep falling slightly for the next 50 years
Rainfall will reach zero within the next ten years
Rainfall will fall by the same amount every year forever
b.why: A short step ahead stays close to the data, so it is the least uncertain. The 50 year prediction is tempting because it follows the same trend, but it is less certain because conditions can change over a long time.
b.clue: Which prediction looks the shortest time ahead?

a.best: Most of these towns lost population over ten years

b.best: Rainfall will keep falling slightly next year

problems.detail: The clue 'Which prediction looks the shortest time ahead?' gives the answer away. Only one option looks one year ahead, so a student can pick it without understanding why short-range predictions are more certain.

The clue 'describes the data already collected and does not claim every case' rules out the two predictions and the 'every' option, which leaves only the right answer. It hands the answer over instead of prompting thinking.

check.summary: The card, remember line and answers are correct. Both clues give the answer away: the clue for b points straight to the shortest time frame, and the clue for a rules out every wrong option.
